title: Are we eating enough protein to age well? Why experts think no
summary: A 2026 perspective in Frontiers in Nutrition argues current protein guidelines aim to prevent deficiency rather than optimize healthy aging. Are the so-called "gym bros" actually onto something when it comes to protein? And could we all benefit from consuming more protein in our diets?

A perspective paper published on June 16, 2026 in Frontiers in Nutrition makes the case for updating current official public health advice for protein intake and exercise.

In the paper, Chris Macdonald, PhD, fellow and lab director at Lucy Cavendish College, University of Cambridge, in the United Kingdom, draws attention to the fact that current recommendations focus on minimum intakes to prevent disease rather than on maximizing long-term health benefits.

An important point from the research compiled is that certain groups of people—namely, physically active adults, older adults, and pregnant people—may benefit from much higher protein intakes than are currently recommended.

The paper argues that our protein intake could be increased to about twice the current minimum recommendations, reaching up to 1 gram per pound (g/lb) of body weight.

For reference, the current guidelines recommend at baseline around 0.75 to 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day (g/kg/day), or roughly about 0.34 to 0.36 g/lb.

The paper also concludes that increasing protein intake offers wide-ranging benefits, including faster muscle recovery, better weight management and fat loss, and reduced risk of fractures.

It’s important to note, however, that federal or international dietary guidelines are designed for the general population and not specific groups, so change is often slow and requires decades of evidence. Nonetheless, the current guidelines could benefit from a review by public health officials.

To discuss how individuals should approach consuming protein and more, Medical News Today spoke to two experts.

Michelle Routhenstein, MS, RD, noted that the current recommended dietary allowance for protein, 0.8 g/kg/day, was established to prevent protein deficiency and "not necessarily to optimize muscle health, healthy aging, or cardiometabolic resilience."

Kristin Kirkpatrick, MS, RDN, said that although current guidelines provide a good starting point, they don’t offer a personalized approach to maximize health and longevity. "Protein needs vary based on factors like age, activity level, health status, and even goals," she said.

Routhenstein emphasized that certain groups—people older than age 40, those taking GLP-1 medications, those trying to lose weight, and people with cardiometabolic diseases like obesity—benefit from higher protein intake. "In my practice, I assess all of those factors to identify an appropriate protein range before we even talk about food choices. . . . That’s why I don’t believe a one-size-fits-all recommendation works for everyone," Kirkpatrick added.

Both experts suggested a practical target range for many adults of about 1.2–1.6 g/kg per day, depending on exercise level, to support lean muscle preservation, metabolic health, satiety and physical function. They stressed that protein is one piece of a heart-healthy dietary pattern.

"Using a 1.2–1.6 g/kg protein target, you can easily get this through a whole foods diet, tailored by which protein sources you enjoy, tolerate, and support your cardiometabolic health," Routhenstein said. For vegans, she recommends ensuring nutrient adequacy via sources like tofu, tempeh, beans and legumes; for omnivores, a mix of animal and plant proteins split across meals.

Kirkpatrick advised spreading protein across meals to hit daily goals: eggs or Greek yogurt at breakfast, lean proteins or legumes at lunch and dinner, and protein-rich snacks such as cottage cheese with berries, roasted chickpeas, edamame, or a protein bar. "For some individuals—especially athletes, people with low appetites, or those taking GLP-1 medications—a protein shake can simply be a convenient way to help meet their needs," she said.

Both experts cautioned that focusing solely on protein can crowd out other important nutrients like vitamin C, potassium, magnesium, folate and fiber. "To avoid this from happening, it is important to focus on protein within the context of the full meal and diet," Routhenstein said. Kirkpatrick added, "Eating more protein shouldn’t mean eating less fiber, fruits, vegetables, or healthy fats."

Safety and source matter. For healthy adults with normal kidney function, Routhenstein said protein intakes up to about 2 g/kg/day appear to be safe, but there is little evidence that routinely eating more than this provides additional health benefits. Very high intakes over the long term may increase the risk of digestive, kidney, or vascular issues for some individuals.

People with chronic kidney disease should follow individualized protein targets, Routhenstein warned: "Excessive protein can place additional stress on the kidneys and may accelerate disease progression."

Kirkpatrick also highlighted the importance of how people raise protein intake. If higher protein comes primarily from processed meats and foods high in saturated fat, it may increase cardiovascular risk. "The goal isn’t simply ‘more protein’; it’s choosing higher-quality protein sources within an overall well-planned heart-healthy diet," she said.

Routhenstein noted that high intakes of animal protein, particularly red and processed meats, can raise levels of TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide), which has been linked to cardiovascular risk. On gut health, she said animal-protein-heavy diets may shift the microbiome toward more gram-negative bacteria, potentially contributing to inflammation and arterial stiffness. Kirkpatrick reiterated that problems are often about what’s missing—low fiber and few plant foods—rather than protein itself.

Exercise remains a central component. "Regular physical activity is one of the most important pillars of longevity," Kirkpatrick said. Combining adequate protein with resistance training and overall activity maximizes benefits for muscle, brain and cardiovascular health, and independence as we age.

In summary, the emerging view among these experts is that many people may benefit from protein intakes above current minimum guidelines, but personalized recommendations, attention to protein quality, and coupling nutrition with exercise are essential to optimize healthy aging and minimize risks.

“Regular physical activity is one of the most important pillars of longevity.
